content: The use of erythromycin carries a potential risk of QT prolongation, a condition that affects the heart's electrical activity and can lead to serious arrhythmias. This risk may be heightened if you are taking certain medications, such as diuretics (commonly referred to as water pills), or if you have medical conditions that result in significant loss of body fluids, such as severe sweating, diarrhea, or vomiting. Erythromycin may interfere with the effectiveness of live bacterial vaccines, such as the typhoid vaccine, potentially reducing their ability to provide immunity. Additionally, some erythromycin formulations may contain sodium, which could be relevant for individuals on sodium-restricted diets. This medication is known to pass into breast milk, so caution is advised for breastfeeding mothers. Drug interactions can alter the way erythromycin or other medications work, potentially increasing the risk of serious side effects. It is important to maintain a comprehensive list of all medications and supplements you are taking, including prescription drugs, over-the-counter products, and herbal supplements, and share this information with your healthcare provider. Certain drugs may affect the removal of erythromycin from your body, altering its effectiveness. Conversely, erythromycin can slow the elimination of other drugs, potentially impacting their function. Erythromycin may interfere with specific laboratory tests, such as urine tests, potentially leading to inaccurate results. If an overdose occurs and the individual experiences severe symptoms such as loss of consciousness or difficulty breathing, emergency services (911) should be contacted immediately. For non-emergency cases, a poison control center should be contacted promptly. In the United States, the poison control hotline is 1-800-222-1222. This medication has been prescribed specifically for your current condition and should not be used for other purposes unless directed by your doctor. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is close to the time of your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and resume your regular dosing schedule. Do not double the dose to catch up. Store erythromycin at room temperature, away from light and moisture. Avoid storing it in the bathroom. Do not dispose of this medication by flushing it down the toilet or pouring it into a drain unless specifically instructed to do so. Properly discard this product when it is expired or no longer needed, following local disposal guidelines. Erythromycin is used to treat a variety of bacterial infections and may also be prescribed to prevent certain bacterial infections. It belongs to a class of antibiotics known as macrolides. This medication is effective only against bacterial infections and will not work for viral infections, such as the common cold or flu. Take erythromycin by mouth as directed by your doctor, usually before a meal. It is best absorbed on an empty stomach. Do not crush the medication, as it has a bitter taste; swallow it whole. The dosage and duration of treatment depend on your medical condition and response to therapy. For optimal results, take this antibiotic at evenly spaced intervals. If you are using it to treat an infection, continue taking it for the full prescribed duration, even if symptoms improve after a few days. Stopping the medication too early may result in a recurrence of the infection. If you are taking it to prevent an infection, follow your doctor’s instructions precisely. Common side effects of erythromycin include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach pain or cramping, and loss of appetite. Taking the medication with food may help alleviate these symptoms. Remember that your doctor has prescribed this medication because they believe the benefits outweigh the risks of side effects. Rarely, erythromycin may cause a severe intestinal condition known as Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea, which can occur during treatment or weeks to months after stopping the medication. Prolonged or repeated use of erythromycin may lead to oral thrush or a new yeast infection. Serious allergic reactions to erythromycin are rare but can occur. Symptoms of an allergic reaction may include rash, itching, swelling (especially of the face, tongue, or throat), severe dizziness, or difficulty breathing. This is not a complete list of possible side effects. In the United States, contact your doctor for medical advice about side effects. In Canada, consult your doctor for guidance. Before taking erythromycin, inform your doctor or pharmacist if you are allergic to it, other macrolide antibiotics (such as azithromycin or clarithromycin), or any other substances. This product may contain inactive ingredients that could cause allergic reactions or other issues. Erythromycin may cause QT prolongation, a condition that affects the heart rhythm. The risk of QT prolongation may be increased if you have certain medical conditions or are taking other drugs that can cause QT prolongation. Low levels of potassium or magnesium in the blood can also increase this risk. This is particularly relevant if you are using diuretics or experiencing conditions such as severe sweating, diarrhea, or vomiting. Erythromycin may reduce the effectiveness of live bacterial vaccines, such as the typhoid vaccine. Some erythromycin products may contain sodium, which should be considered for individuals on sodium-restricted diets. This medication passes into breast milk, so breastfeeding mothers should consult their healthcare provider before use. Always consult your healthcare professional for complete information about this medication and your specific health needs.
